set.story: In a later legend, best known from the Roman poet Statius, the sea goddess Thetis dipped her baby son Achilles in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel. That one untouched spot was where an arrow later struck and killed him at Troy.

why: The Styx-dipping story is not attested in Greek sources before the Roman poet Statius (1st c. AD); 'later Greek and Roman tellings' overstates the Greek attestation.

set.story: Cupid was the Roman god of love, usually shown as a winged boy with a bow. Anyone struck by one of his golden arrows fell in love.

why: In Ovid not all of Cupid's arrows cause love: the lead-tipped one makes the victim flee love (Apollo and Daphne). Specified the golden arrows.
'Malik decided to go the extra mile and invited both ... coworkers' also fills the cloze grammatically and sensibly.

set.story: This principle of equal punishment appears in the laws of the Hebrew Bible (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the even older Code of Hammurabi. Jesus later quotes it in the Sermon on the Mount, telling his followers not to retaliate.

why: Matthew 5:38-39 teaches non-retaliation ('resist not evil', turn the other cheek), not forgiveness as such; reworded to match the text.

set.story: In Hinduism, Buddhism, and Sikhism, a guru is a spiritual teacher or guide; the word is Sanskrit. In Sikhism, the title belongs to the ten human Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, and to the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib.

why: Sikhism has ten human Gurus in succession; only Guru Nanak founded the faith, so 'ten founding Gurus' is inaccurate.
'the self-styled financial Einstein, who claims his system never fails' also fits the cloze sensibly.
'Benefactor' means a patron who gives money or support, not a stranger who helps someone in trouble; not a true synonym.
Seventh heaven (state of bliss) overlaps the def 'place or situation where someone expects to find happiness'; risky as a wrong option for question (b).
'The quiet engineer and the outgoing salesman were the be-all and end-all of the startup' also fills the cloze grammatically and plausibly.
'Svengali' (one person who controls another) and 'rabble-rouser' (agitator) are not synonyms of a charismatic leader who lures followers into trouble; 'charmer' is too weak.

ex: Our coach is a real Jekyll and Hyde: friendly at practice, furious on game day.
Wei is gentle and polite at the office, but his Jekyll and Hyde switch behind the wheel shocks his carpool.

why: Original ex 2 ('shocked his calm, polite coworkers') attached 'calm, polite' to the coworkers, so the sentence did not show Wei's two sides.

set.story: Peter Pan, created by J. M. Barrie, first appeared in his 1902 novel The Little White Bird and became famous through the 1904 play and later novel, as a boy who lives in Neverland and refuses ever to grow up.

why: Peter Pan first appeared in The Little White Bird (1902), not in the 1904 play; the story said he was 'created ... in a 1904 play'.

set.story: In Dr. Seuss's 1957 book How the Grinch Stole Christmas!, a grumpy, Christmas-hating creature tries to stop the holiday by stealing the Whos' presents, trees, and decorations. The book did not show him as green; the 1966 TV cartoon made him green.

why: Factual error: the Grinch is not green in the 1957 book (drawn in black and white with red); Chuck Jones made him green for the 1966 TV special.
'...the hotel lost our booking—karma in full effect' is a plausible fill for the cloze.

set.story: In Patrick Hamilton's 1938 play Gas Light and the 1944 film Gaslight, a husband tries to convince his wife she is going insane. When the gas lamps dim, because he is secretly searching a sealed-off part of the house by gaslight, he insists she is imagining things.

why: In the play and film the lamps dim as a side effect of the husband secretly lighting the gas in the closed-off upstairs flat or attic while he searches it; he does not deliberately dim them, though he does insist she is imagining things.
'Fatima felt she was stuck in the Twilight Zone' fits the cloze grammatically and is arguably sensible; the endlessly repeated day is itself a Twilight-Zone-style premise.
'Spotting my red suitcase ... felt like playing Sherlock Holmes' (playing detective) also fits the cloze sensibly.
'a maverick move that worked—for a while' fits the cloze grammatically; maverick is common attributively.

set.story: The prologue to Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet calls the pair “star-crossed lovers,” meaning thwarted by the stars, or fate. Born into two feuding families, they fall in love, and the romance ends in both their deaths.

why: Original sentence ('meaning thwarted by the stars ... since their feuding families doom their romance') muddled the meaning of star-crossed with the cause of the feud; clarified.

set.story: A wild-goose chase was a 16th-century horseback game in which riders had to follow a leader's unpredictable course. Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet has the earliest known figurative use, when Mercutio compares a battle of wits to it; the 'hopeless search' sense came later.

why: Factual error: the term appears in print earlier, in Gervase Markham's 1593 horsemanship book, before Romeo and Juliet (printed 1597). Shakespeare's is only the earliest figurative use, and Mercutio uses it to describe a battle of wits, not for the game itself.

set.story: The line “In the future everybody will be world famous for fifteen minutes” is credited to artist Andy Warhol and was printed in the catalog of his 1968 exhibition in Stockholm, though who actually coined it has been questioned.

why: Corrected the quote to the catalog's actual wording ('fifteen', not '15') and avoided implying the catalog was its first appearance (a 1967 Time article had already credited the idea to Warhol).
'a truly Mickey Mouse situation' (badly run bureaucracy) is a plausible fill for the cloze about offices giving contradictory requirements.

set.story: The idea goes back to Plato's dialogue the Symposium, which describes love rising from physical attraction toward a love of wisdom and beauty itself; the Renaissance scholar Marsilio Ficino coined the Latin term amor platonicus, “Platonic love.”

why: Ficino coined the Latin 'amor platonicus'; the English phrase 'Platonic love' came later.
'it became a boycott that changed the whole school' fits the cloze grammatically and is semi-plausible; boycott is also directly tied to the Rosa Parks story.
